title: は vs が

taeKim.title: Introduction to particles (は, も, が)

summary: は sets the stage ("as for X…"). が points at the one doing or being the thing — often the new information.
explanation: Think of は as a spotlight on the **stage**. It says what we're talking about, and the rest of the sentence comments on it. The topic is usually something already in the conversation: you, the weather, the thing you're both looking at.
が points at **who or what** fills the slot. It answers the question "who?" or "which one?" — so it tends to carry the new information.
Three rules of thumb that cover most real situations:
**1. Question words take が, never は.** {誰|だれ}が, {何|なに}が, どれが. You can't make an unknown thing the topic — you don't know what it is yet. Answers to those questions take が too.
**2. New observations take が.** You look outside and it's raining: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っています. You're reporting something that just entered the scene.
**3. は can mean "at least this one" (contrast).** {雨|あめ}は{降|ふ}っていますが… — "It IS raining, but…" The は quietly sets the rain against something else.
Bonus: {好|す}き, {嫌|きら}い, {上手|じょうず}, わかる and できる mark the thing liked/understood with が: {猫|ねこ}が{好|す}きです.

examples.note: You are the topic; your name is the comment.

examples.ja: {田中|たなか}さんが{来|き}ました。
あ、{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っています。
{私|わたし}はラーメンが{好|す}きです。
examples.note: は for you (the topic), が for the thing liked.

a.ja: タイラーは{曲|きょく}を{書|か}きます。

b.ja: タイラーが{曲|きょく}を{書|か}きます。
b.en: Tyler is the one who writes the music.

contrasts.why: With は you're telling us something about Tyler. With が you're answering "who writes the music?" — the spotlight is on Tyler being the one.

b.en: THIS is the station (the one you're looking for).

contrasts.why: は describes "here." が picks "here" out of other possible places — like pointing at a map and saying "this one."

b.ja: {雨|あめ}は{降|ふ}っていますが、{寒|さむ}くないです。
b.en: It is raining, but it isn't cold.

contrasts.why: が just reports the rain. は sets the rain up against something else — you can feel the "but" coming.

exercises.prompt: {誰|だれ}＿ピアノを{弾|ひ}きますか。

options.why: 誰 is a question word, and question words always take が. You're asking who fills the "plays piano" slot.
は would make 誰 the topic — "as for who…" — but you can't set an unknown person on the stage. Question words never take は.
を marks the thing being acted on. The piano is already marked with を; 誰 is the one doing the playing.

exercises.scene: You're introducing yourself to the Studio Kura staff.
exercises.prompt: {私|わたし}＿タイラーです。よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
exercises.en: I'm Tyler. Nice to meet you.

options.why: You're the topic, and your name is the new information about you. This is the standard self-introduction.
Grammatical, but it means "I'm the one who's Tyler" — what you'd say if someone asked "Which of you is Tyler?"
を marks an object of an action, and です isn't an action. There's nothing for を to attach to.

exercises.prompt: {私|わたし}はラーメン＿{好|す}きです。

options.why: 好き is an adjective, not a verb. The thing you like is marked with が: ラーメンが好き.
Possible, but it adds contrast: "Ramen, I like (other things, not so much)." Natural in the right moment, not as a plain statement.
を needs an action verb. 好き describes a state, so the liked thing takes が.

exercises.scene: You're looking at a map with a station attendant and point at a spot.
exercises.prompt: すみません、ここ＿{一貴山|いきさん}{駅|えき}ですか。
exercises.en: Excuse me, is this Ikisan Station?

options.why: "Here" is the topic and you're asking what it is. Plain and natural.
This asks "Is HERE the Ikisan Station?" — picking this spot out from others. Works if you're comparing spots on the map, but it's not the default.

exercises.scene: Tell Ranko's family that you like cats.
exercises.why: Topic first (私は), then the thing liked with が, then 好きです.

exercises.scene: Susanna asks who's making dinner tonight. Say that you'll make it.
exercises.why: She asked "who?", so the answer takes が. 僕が作るよ is relaxed and natural between partners.
